New Jersey law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • 30 years' actual possession of real estate (other than woodlands or uncultivated tracts), uninterruptedly continued by occupancy, descent, conveyance or otherwise, vests full title in the possessor and bars recovery actions, however the possession began. (N.J.S.A. 2A:14-30; source)
  • 60 years' actual possession is required for woodlands or uncultivated tracts. (N.J.S.A. 2A:14-30; source)

New Jersey Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my New Jersey house?

Check the statute and talk to a New Jersey attorney about your facts.

Does long-term occupation ever turn into ownership under New Jersey law?

Only after a very long period of possession. New Jersey's adverse possession statutes, N.J.S.A. 2A:14-30 and 2A:14-31, vest title in a possessor after 30 years of actual possession of real estate, or 60 years for woodlands and uncultivated tracts. Those periods are the ones the Legislature's own bill statement describes.

The same bill statement points out a tension. Other statutes, N.J.S.A. 2A:14-6 and 2A:14-7, set 20-year limits for entering or suing over land. The New Jersey Supreme Court addressed the conflict in J & M Land Co. v. First Union National Bank, 166 N.J. 493 (2001), where a company with 39 years of possession of uncultivated land lost because the 60-year period applied. A 2012 bill (A1551) proposed 20 years in most cases and 30 years for woodlands and would have repealed the two older sections, but a bill that was only introduced does not change the law. Check the Legislature's statutes page for the current text before relying on any number.

Does a short stay in someone's New Jersey house create ownership rights?

No. A person who moves into a vacant house gains no title by the mere passage of months or a few years, because the period the Legislature's bill statement describes for ordinary real estate is 30 years of actual possession. What a short occupancy can create is a practical problem. The owner may have to go to court to remove the occupant, and the route depends on whether the person is a tenant.

Public land has its own rule. According to the bill statement, the Supreme Court in Devins v. Borough of Bogota, 124 N.J. 570 (1991), held that municipally owned property that is neither dedicated to nor used for a public purpose can be taken by adverse possession. A private owner's house is a different case, but the point shows that who holds title affects the analysis.

When does an occupant count as a tenant in New Jersey?

That question controls the removal process. The NJ Courts explain that two statutes cover eviction. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 applies to commercial tenants and to residential properties with no more than two rental units, such as a two-family house, or a three-family house where the landlord lives in one unit. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and the sections that follow apply to the other residential tenants, with exceptions for hotels, motels and seasonal renters.

The Judiciary states the central rule: residential tenants can be evicted only by a Special Civil Part officer, and only after the landlord files a landlord tenant case and gets a judgment for possession. Changing locks, padlocking doors or cutting off gas, water or electricity is an illegal lockout. A tenant who is locked out can file a complaint in the Special Civil Part asking to return and for damages. If a person lives in your house and you are unsure whether they count as a tenant, phone the clerk of the Special Civil Part for your county and ask which filing fits before you act.

How does a lawful eviction work in New Jersey?

After a judgment for possession, a landlord waits three business days and may then apply for a warrant of removal. The warrant costs $35 plus the officer's mileage fee, and a second mileage fee may apply if the officer must return. A residential tenant gets at least three business days after service to leave. If the tenant stays, the landlord arranges the lockout with the officer, and the officer's fee cannot be greater than $75.

  • A landlord has 30 days from the judgment to apply for the warrant unless a court order or written agreement stops it.
  • The officer then has 30 days from issuance to carry it out.
  • The complaint must attach the lease or its relevant pages and a Registration Statement for the rental unless exempt under N.J.S.A. 46:8-27.
  • A tenant who owes only rent can restore the tenancy by paying everything due up to three business days after eviction.
  • A tenant can seek an Order for Orderly Removal, usually up to seven calendar days, or a hardship stay of up to six months if all rent is paid.

Filing fees for the complaint are $50 for one defendant and $5 for each extra defendant, plus a $7 service fee. A landlord that is a corporation, LLC or LLP must use a New Jersey attorney.

Which rules apply to occupants in a foreclosed New Jersey home?

Foreclosure does not erase a lease. The NJ Courts say a bona fide residential tenant in good standing is not forced out because the building is in foreclosure, and whoever wins the sheriff auction inherits the lease and the tenant's rights. Renters in a foreclosed building may be protected by N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 to 61.12, and the court advises tenants who receive a complaint to see an attorney and to show the lender's lawyer a copy of the lease.

For an owner occupant, the process differs. After the sheriff sale, the buyer must obtain a Writ of Possession, and the sheriff tells the defendant the date to leave. Morris County's sale terms state that properties are sold subject to the rights of occupants or tenants, so a bidder takes on that risk.

What should a New Jersey owner do about an unwanted occupant?

Move through the court rather than around it. The most reliable steps are these:

  • Gather the deed, tax bills and any lease, text messages or receipts showing how the person came to be there.
  • Do not change locks or shut off utilities on someone who may be a tenant, because that can create liability for an illegal lockout.
  • Ask the Special Civil Part clerk for your county which complaint matches the facts.
  • Call Legal Services of New Jersey at 1-888-LSNJ-LAW or a lawyer referral service if a lawyer is out of reach.

Keep records of when the person moved in and what rent, if any, was ever accepted. Those facts decide whether the case belongs under the tenant statutes.

What does an occupant or a possession claim mean for a sale?

An occupied house carries extra risk for any buyer. Morris County's sheriff sale terms, for example, sell property subject to the rights of occupants or tenants, and a bidder must then go to court for a Writ of Possession. A private seller can ease that concern by keeping the deed, tax bills and any lease or rent records together, so the buyer's attorney can see who has a right to be in the house.

SituationRuleSource
Adverse possession, ordinary land30 years of actual possessionN.J.S.A. 2A:14-30
Adverse possession, woodlands or uncultivated tracts60 yearsN.J.S.A. 2A:14-31
Residential tenant removalJudgment for possession, then warrant of removal by a Special Civil Part officerNJ Courts landlord tenant page
Tenant in a foreclosed buildingTenancy continues; auction winner takes over the leaseNJ Courts landlord tenant page

Source: Assembly bill A1551 statement and NJ Courts landlord tenant self-help.

More questions about New Jersey Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long must someone occupy a New Jersey house before claiming title?

The statutes the Legislature describes require 30 years of actual possession for ordinary real estate and 60 years for woodlands or uncultivated tracts. Confirm the current text of N.J.S.A. 2A:14-30 and 2A:14-31 with an attorney.

Can I change the locks on someone living in my New Jersey property?

Not if they may be a tenant. The NJ Courts say changing locks or cutting utilities is an illegal lockout, and only a Special Civil Part officer can carry out an eviction.

Who removes a tenant after a New Jersey court orders eviction?

A Special Civil Part officer. The landlord obtains a judgment for possession, waits three business days, applies for a warrant of removal and the officer serves it and carries out any lockout.

Does foreclosure end a tenant's lease in New Jersey?

Generally no. A residential tenant with a valid lease in good standing keeps their rights, and the winning bidder inherits the lease.

What does the New Jersey Supreme Court case J & M Land say about adverse possession?

It held that the 60-year period applied to uncultivated land, so a company with 39 years of possession lost. The Legislature's bill statement cites the case as the reason the statutes are unclear.

New Jersey Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Cash Home Buyers in New Jersey

  • Turn the New Jersey Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

New Jersey statutes set the basic rules between landlords and tenants, including deposits, notices and what happens when a rental is sold.

What the official sources say

  • Annual additional security collected may not exceed 10 percent of the current security deposit. (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.2 (DCA Security Deposit Law PDF); source)
  • Within 30 days after lease termination the owner must return the deposit plus the tenant's share of interest, less lawful charges, by personal delivery or registered/certified mail. (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1 (DCA Security Deposit Law PDF); source)
  • In a tenant suit for wrongly withheld deposit, the court awards double the amount plus full costs and, in its discretion, reasonable attorney's fees. (N.J.S.A. 46:8-21.1; source)
  • Landlord may not serve a notice to quit or sue for possession as reprisal for the tenant enforcing lease/legal rights, a good-faith complaint to a government authority about health/safety violations, or tenant organizing; refusing to renew without cause counts as substantial alteration. (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.10; source)
  • A notice to quit or substantial change in tenancy without cause after such protected acts creates a rebuttable presumption of reprisal; no presumption arises from non-renewal if the tenant's request came sooner than 90 days before lease expiration. (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-10.12; source)
  • A notice to quit is a condition precedent to raising rent in a periodic tenancy (annotation to 2A:18-61.2 citing case law). (DCA annotated N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1/61.2 PDF; source)
Selling in New Jersey?
We buy New Jersey houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which New Jersey statute applies to a rented house?

The answer turns on the size and use of the building. The New Jersey Courts landlord-tenant page explains that N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 governs commercial space, residential buildings with at most two rental units, and a three-family house where the owner occupies one unit. Nearly all other residential rentals fall under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and the sections that follow, known as the Anti-Eviction Act. Hotels, motels and seasonal rentals sit outside it.

Landlord-tenant lawsuits start in the Special Civil Part of Superior Court, at the courthouse serving the rental's county. Corporations, LLCs and limited partnerships must be represented by a New Jersey attorney. Sole owners and general partners may speak for themselves. Before putting a tenant-occupied house on the market, an owner should decide which of the two statutes covers it, since that determines the notice periods discussed below.

Does selling the house let the owner remove a tenant?

Not by itself. Under the Anti-Eviction Act a covered tenant may be removed only for a cause the statute lists, and signing a sale contract with an investor is not on that list. The buyer simply takes over as landlord under the existing lease.

Two sale-linked grounds do exist. An owner of a building with three residential units or fewer may recover a unit after contracting to sell it to a buyer who intends to live there, if the contract requires the unit to be empty at closing. For condominium and cooperative units, a similar ground reaches tenants whose tenancy began after the master deed was recorded, but only when the tenant received the disclosure statement required by N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.9. The remaining grounds include:

  • nonpayment of rent, or chronic late payment after a written warning
  • disorderly behavior or intentional damage to the premises
  • continued violation of reasonable house rules or lease terms after a written warning
  • refusal of reasonable lease changes when a term ends
  • permanent retirement of the building from residential use
  • conversion to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership

In short, a seller whose buyer wants vacant possession needs either the small-building own-use ground or the tenant's cooperation.

What written notice must precede an eviction suit?

The required lead time ranges from three days to three years, depending on the ground. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 requires a written demand that describes the cause in detail. It may be handed to the tenant, left with a household member over 14 at the tenant's home, or mailed by certified mail, with a regular-mail copy if the certified letter is not picked up. Plain nonpayment cases are exempt from this requirement.

Lead time under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2
GroundNotice period
Disorderly conduct, damage to the unit, or certain drug-offense grounds3 days
House-rule or lease violations, habitual late rent, refused lease changes1 month
Owner must board up, demolish or correct cited violations3 months
Own-use or sale-for-occupancy grounds2 months, and no suit before a written lease ends
Permanent retirement of the building18 months, and no suit before the lease expires
Conversion to condominium or cooperative3 years, and no suit before the lease expires

Source: N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2, as published by the Department of Community Affairs.

Who keeps the tenant's security deposit after a sale?

The buyer ends up holding it, and the seller must move it. N.J.S.A. 46:8-20 directs an owner who conveys a rental to pass the deposit and the tenant's accrued interest to the grantee when the deed is delivered or within five days afterward, then to tell the tenant by registered or certified mail who the new holder is and where to reach them. The buyer has its own duty to demand those funds from the seller.

Once the money is turned over, N.J.S.A. 46:8-21 frees the seller from liability to the tenant. The buyer stays answerable for proper investment, notices, interest and the eventual refund, whether or not the seller ever sent the funds. Other rules from the Security Deposit Law that a seller's file should reflect:

  • the deposit is capped at one and a half months of rent, and yearly increases are limited to 10 percent of the existing deposit
  • the tenant gets written notice of the bank, account type, rate and amount, repeated after any change of ownership
  • no deductions are allowed while the tenant still lives in the unit
  • the refund, with itemized charges, is due a month after the lease ends
  • a tenant who proves wrongful withholding recovers double plus costs, and claims up to $5,000 go to small claims

An owner-occupied building with two or fewer rental units is outside the law unless the tenant gives 30 days' written notice invoking it.

What does the court process look like step by step?

Removal requires a judge and a court officer, and a landlord who bypasses either has locked the tenant out illegally. The landlord files a verified complaint with a case information statement, the lease and a registration statement. Court-listed charges are $50 for one tenant and $5 for each additional one, plus a $7 service charge. The first trial date falls at least 21 days after the summons is served.

Tenants must come to court, because written answers are not accepted. A missing landlord means dismissal, and a missing tenant means default. If both show up, court staff first offer a settlement conference, and the judge hears the case only if that fails. A win for the landlord produces a judgment for possession, which leads to these steps:

  • a three-business-day wait before the landlord may ask for a warrant of removal, which costs $35 plus mileage
  • service of the warrant by a court officer, who allows a residential tenant three business days to leave
  • a 30-day window to apply for the warrant after judgment, unless a court order or signed agreement pauses it

In rent cases, a tenant who pays everything owed plus lawful costs stops the process, even up to three business days after being removed, and a landlord who refuses risks a $500 penalty. Tenants may also seek up to seven days of orderly removal, or a hardship stay of up to six months with all rent paid.

Which defenses and protections can slow a sale of a tenant-occupied home?

A buyer will ask about these before closing. The Courts page describes the Marini Doctrine of habitability: a tenant who pays the rent into court may argue that heat, hot water, a working toilet or safe stairways were missing. That argument cannot be used to excuse repeated late payment or lease violations.

Registration is another checkpoint. A small owner-occupied building registers with the Community Development Authority, and every other rental registers with the Bureau of Housing Inspection. The statement goes in with the complaint. Tenants can also argue the tenancy is illegal, for example an unapproved extra apartment, or ask for a rent abatement. When a public agency subsidizes the rent, the landlord must notify that agency and attach proof.

A foreclosure does not wipe out a lease. A tenant in good standing is not forced to move, and whoever buys at the sheriff's sale takes the building subject to the tenant's rights.

What paperwork should an owner assemble first?

Gather what a title agent and buyer will request. Call the Special Civil Part office serving the property for its current fee schedule, because court charges change, and ask the municipal clerk whether a local rental license applies.

  • every signed lease and renewal, with a rent roll
  • deposit notices and the bank statement showing where each deposit sits
  • the rental registration statement
  • any notice to cease, notice to quit or court filing
  • repair requests and invoices

An owner who needs the house empty has two honest options: wait for the lease to run out and negotiate a move-out date, or sell to a buyer who takes the tenancy as is.

More questions about New Jersey Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

Can a New Jersey landlord shut off utilities to push a tenant out?

No. Changing locks, padlocking doors or cutting gas, water or electricity is illegal. A tenant locked out this way can file in the Special Civil Part and ask to be let back in, along with money damages.

What happens to a lease when the owner sells in New Jersey?

The lease generally carries on. A buyer steps into the landlord's position, and the only sale-based exception is a buyer who will personally live in a unit of a building with three or fewer units and wants it empty at closing.

How soon must a deposit be refunded?

Within 30 days after the lease ends, delivered in person or by registered or certified mail, with the tenant's share of interest and an itemized list of any deductions. Wrongful withholding can cost the landlord double the amount.

Can a tenant keep the home after a judgment for possession?

Sometimes. In a nonpayment case, paying all rent and costs within three business days of the judgment or the eviction ends it. A hardship stay can last up to six months, and orderly removal up to seven days.

Does an LLC landlord need a lawyer in landlord-tenant court?

Yes. Corporations, LLCs and limited partnerships must be represented by a New Jersey attorney, while sole proprietors and general partners may represent themselves.

title: New Jersey Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
New Jersey Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in New Jersey
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Jersey Eviction Notice Rules sale

Selling a New Jersey House? Get a Cash Offer

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

New Jersey law requires a landlord to give a specific written notice before filing an eviction, and the number of days depends on the reason.

What the official sources say

  • Nonpayment of rent is a ground for removal under 2A:18-61.1(a), and 2A:18-61.2 excepts nonpayment (subsections a. or f.) from the written notice-to-quit requirement. (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1(a); 2A:18-61.2; source)
  • Notice before suit: 3 days for disorderly conduct or injury to premises; 1 month for continued rules violation, substantial breach of covenant, or habitual failure to pay rent; 3 months for subsection g. grounds. (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2(a)-(c); source)
  • Notice must specify in detail the cause of termination; no judgment of possession without written demand and notice (except nonpayment). (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2; source)
  • Landlord-tenant cases are filed in the Special Civil Part of Superior Court. (NJ Courts, Landlord/Tenant; source)
Selling in New Jersey?
We buy New Jersey houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What notice must a New Jersey landlord give before filing an eviction?

It depends on the reason. Under the Anti-Eviction Act, N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 and following, a landlord who wants a judgment for possession of a New Jersey rental generally must make a written demand and give written notice first, and the length of that notice runs from three days to three years. Unpaid rent is the main exception.

The Department of Community Affairs summarizes the rule in its Landlord-Tenant Information Service bulletin: every good cause eviction other than nonpayment needs a written Notice to Quit that describes the cause. A Notice to Quit ends the tenancy on paper, but the tenant does not have to leave until a court enters a judgment for possession.

For an owner thinking about selling a rented house, the order matters. The notice period has to run before the complaint is filed, so a sale timeline that depends on a vacant house has to start with the correct notice on the correct date.

Does a New Jersey landlord need a notice before suing for unpaid rent?

No, with one common exception. Nonpayment of rent is ground a. of N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1, and N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 excuses the written demand and notice for that ground. The landlord can file in the Special Civil Part right away.

The DCA bulletin adds that a tenant in federally subsidized housing is owed a 14-day notice before suit. It also says a tenant cannot be evicted for nonpayment when the unpaid portion of rent went to keep electric, gas, water or sewer service on after the utility warned of shutoff because the landlord had not paid it.

A tenant who owes rent keeps a way out even after suit begins. The NJ Courts landlord-tenant page says the case may be dismissed if the tenant pays all rent due plus court costs by 4:30 p.m. on the trial date.

How many days or months of notice does each ground require?

The statute sets the minimum for each ground, and the table pulls the common ones together. A court can reject a complaint if the landlord gave a shorter notice than the ground requires, so the count matters.

Minimum notice before filing, from N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 as reprinted by the NJ Department of Community Affairs
GroundSubsection of 2A:18-61.1Notice before suit
Disorderly conduct, property damage, drug or assault offenses, theft findingsb, c, m, n, o, p3 days
Rule violations, lease covenant breach, habitual late rentd, e, j1 month
Refusing reasonable new lease termsi1 month
Unpaid rent increase after valid noticef1 month
Owner or buyer will occupy (three units or fewer)l2 months, after the lease ends
Board-up, demolition or code complianceg3 months
Permanent retirement from residential useh18 months, after the lease ends
Condominium or co-op conversionk3 years, after the lease ends

For the one-month grounds, the DCA bulletin also says the notice should be given on or before the start of a new month.

What does a Notice to Cease do, and how is it different from a Notice to Quit?

A Notice to Cease is a warning, and a Notice to Quit is the step that ends the tenancy. Several grounds require both, in that order.

  • Notice to Cease: tells the tenant to stop the conduct, such as disorderly behavior, breaking house rules, or paying late again and again.
  • Notice to Quit: follows if the conduct continues, and it starts the clock for the 3-day or 1-month period in the table.
  • Notice of rent increase: for a rent increase dispute, the landlord must serve a valid Notice to Quit together with notice of the increase before suing over the unpaid amount.

The DCA bulletin notes that courts treat habitual late payment as more than one late payment after the Notice to Cease. It also says a landlord who keeps accepting late rent has to keep warning the tenant that further late payments will lead to eviction, or the original warning can be treated as waived.

What must the notice say, and how can it be delivered?

The notice must state the cause of termination in detail. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2 says that for every ground it covers, the notice shall specify in detail the cause, so a vague line about breaking the lease is a weak foundation for a case.

Delivery has three accepted routes in the reprinted statute.

  • Hand a copy to the tenant or person in possession.
  • Leave a copy at the tenant's usual home with a family member older than 14.
  • Send it by certified mail, and if the certified letter is not claimed, follow with regular mail.

The NJ Courts self-help page adds that, for any case other than unpaid rent, the landlord must attach every notice sent to the tenant to the verified complaint when filing. A landlord who skipped a required notice will have nothing to attach.

Which New Jersey rentals fall outside these notice rules?

The Anti-Eviction Act does not cover every rental. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 carves out owner-occupied premises with no more than two rental units, hotels, motels and guesthouses rented to transient guests or seasonal tenants, and certain units held for a family member with a developmental disability.

Those cases fall under N.J.S.A. 2A:18-53 instead, the same statute the NJ Courts site points to for commercial tenants. For a disorderly tenant or one who destroys or damages the property, that older statute calls for a written notice demanding the tenant leave within three days of service. Holdover cases after a lease ends need a demand and written notice for delivery of possession.

A landlord who owns a two-family house and lives upstairs is therefore working under a different notice scheme than the owner of a three-unit building who lives elsewhere. Confirm which statute applies before serving anything.

Can a landlord raise the rent or change lease terms with a notice?

Yes, but not in the middle of a lease term. The DCA Truth in Renting guide says New Jersey has no statewide rent control, and that a landlord who wants to raise rent must end the old lease and offer a new one at the higher rent, with written notice that the tenant may stay by signing it.

Local law can add limits. The guide says a municipality may adopt a rent control or rent leveling ordinance and that the town's rent control board or municipal clerk can say whether a unit is covered. It also says an increase cannot be unconscionable, a fact-based test that looks at the size of the increase, the landlord's expenses, and rents for similar properties nearby.

The grounds list in 2A:18-61.1 also lets a landlord seek removal of a tenant who refuses reasonable changes to lease terms at renewal, after written notice and the one-month period.

What notice applies when the owner or a buyer wants to move in?

Two months, and only after the lease expires. Subsection l.(3) of N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.1 lets the owner of a building with three residential units or fewer seek possession to occupy a unit, or because a contract of sale calls for the unit to be vacant at closing and the buyer will live there.

The DCA bulletin sets the notice for that ground at two months before suit, with no action until the lease runs out. The same pattern applies to some condominium and co-op units. A tenant who vacates on this kind of notice has a damages claim if the owner then fails to occupy for at least six months, since N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6 allows treble damages plus attorney fees in that situation.

Sellers of larger rented buildings and sellers who want the house empty for an investor buyer do not get this shortcut. For them, the tenancy continues until one of the listed grounds is proved in court.

What happens to a tenant's notice rights when the house is sold?

They carry over to the new owner. N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.3(b) says a tenant covered by the Act cannot be removed by the landlord's successor in ownership except for good cause, a federal-law override, or an eminent domain or code enforcement proceeding.

The NJ Courts site adds that a landlord must notify the tenant in writing about the security deposit account, including when ownership or control of the property transfers. The deposit itself, capped at one and a half months of rent, stays tied to the tenancy.

A buyer purchasing a tenant-occupied house is buying that tenancy with it. Buyers who want a vacant property can offer the tenant a negotiated move-out, but New Jersey requires the tenant to leave only through a court judgment and a Special Civil Part officer.

More questions about New Jersey Eviction Notice Rules

Is a verbal notice enough to start an eviction in New Jersey?

No. The Anti-Eviction Act calls for written demand and written notice, delivered by hand, left at the tenant's home with a family member over 14, or sent by certified mail. A landlord without a written notice has nothing to attach to the complaint.

Can a landlord evict without any notice for unpaid rent?

Yes, in most cases. Nonpayment is excused from the written notice requirement in N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.2. The exception in the DCA bulletin is federally subsidized housing, which needs a 14-day notice before suit.

Does a 3-day notice mean the tenant must leave in 3 days?

No. The 3 days is the minimum wait before the landlord may file suit on grounds such as disorderly conduct or damage. The tenant stays until a judge enters a judgment for possession and a court officer carries out a warrant of removal.

How long does a landlord have to wait to evict a tenant for habitual late rent?

One month. After a written Notice to Cease and continued late payment, the landlord serves a Notice to Quit and waits one month before filing, according to the DCA grounds bulletin and 2A:18-61.2.

Can a landlord evict a tenant because the owner is selling the house?

Only in narrow cases. A building with three residential units or fewer can be cleared on two months' notice if the buyer will live there and the contract calls for a vacant unit. Otherwise a sale alone is not good cause, and the buyer takes the property subject to the tenancy.
